summary: Defines a TLS extension to fix a renegotiation attack in which an attacker connects to a server, injects content, and then splices in a new connection from a victim. The extension cryptographically ties a renegotiation to the earlier handshake. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a TLS connection changes its keys in the middle, the new handshake is not tied to the old one in any way a computer can check. This RFC adds a short piece of data that carries the previous handshake's result, so that both ends can tell a real renegotiation from one that an attacker has spliced in.

questions: what is the tls renegotiation indication extension
how was the tls renegotiation attack fixed
how does tls prevent the renegotiation attack
subtitle: A TLS extension that ties each renegotiation to the connection it happened on, closing a splicing attack.

tldr.problem: A TLS renegotiation is a new handshake inside an existing connection, but nothing in TLS cryptographically links the two, so an attacker can slip their own conversation in front of the client's.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a renegotiation_info extension that carries the verify data of the previous handshake. A server and client that both support it can tell a genuine renegotiation from a spliced one, because the values will not match.
tldr.outcome: Servers should not let clients renegotiate without the extension, and many servers can remove the risk simply by refusing to renegotiate at all.

today: RFC 5746 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates the TLS specifications in RFC 5246 and RFC 4346 and the related documents RFC 4366, RFC 4347 and RFC 2246, and it registers both the extension type and the signalling cipher suite value.

sections.title: The Renegotiation Attack
sections.content:
TLS allows either the client or the server to start a renegotiation, which is a new handshake that establishes new cryptographic parameters. Although the new handshake is carried out using the parameters established by the original handshake, there is no cryptographic binding between the two. That opens the way to an attack in which an attacker who can intercept a client's transport layer connection injects traffic of his own as a prefix to the client's interaction with the server.

The attack works like this. The attacker forms a TLS connection to the server and sends traffic of his choice, which may be several requests and responses at the application layer or simply a partial request intended to prefix the client's data. He then lets the client's TLS handshake proceed with the server. The handshake is in the clear to the attacker but encrypted over the attacker's own connection to the server. Once it completes, the client talks to the server under the new parameters. The attacker cannot read that traffic, but the server believes the initial traffic to and from the attacker is the same as the traffic to and from the client.

With certificate-based client authentication, the server sees a stream of bytes where the first bytes are protected but not authenticated by TLS and the later bytes are authenticated and bound to the client's certificate. In some protocols, notably HTTPS, no distinction is made between the stages before and after authentication and the bytes are handled uniformly, so the server believes the initial traffic belongs to the authenticated client. Even without client certificates, an attacker may be able to have the server accept its data as the client's, for instance by having HTTPS with HTTP cookies where the attacker generates a request of his own that is validated by the client's cookie.

Some protocols, such as IMAP and SMTP, have explicit transitions between authenticated and unauthenticated phases and require the protocol state machine to be partly or fully reset at such transitions, which may limit the effect of these attacks. There is, however, no requirement for state machine resets at TLS renegotiation, so a window of vulnerability remains: prefixing a command that writes to an area visible to the attacker with a client command that includes the client's password would make that password visible to the attacker. Similar attacks exist with SMTP and do not necessarily require the attacker to have an account.

These attacks are possible because the client sends unsolicited authentication information without requiring any specific data from the server. Protocols that require a round trip over TLS before the client sends sensitive information are likely to be less vulnerable.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can open his own encrypted connection to a server, send whatever he likes, and then let the real client's handshake through. The server sees one long stream and cannot tell that the first part came from someone else, so it treats the attacker's words as if the client had sent them.

sections.title: The Extra State Each Side Keeps
sections.content:
Both the client and the server need to store three additional values for each TLS connection state. These values are specific to the connection, not to a session cache entry.

The first is a secure_renegotiation flag, saying whether secure renegotiation is in use for this connection. The second is client_verify_data, the verify data from the Finished message sent by the client on the immediately previous handshake; for the currently defined TLS versions and cipher suites this is a 12-byte value, and for SSLv3 it is a 36-byte value. The third is server_verify_data, the verify data from the Finished message sent by the server on the immediately previous handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of the connection keeps three things: whether the safe form of renegotiation is in use, and the two values that the previous handshake ended with. The new handshake quotes those values back, and that is what proves the two handshakes belong together.

sections.title: The renegotiation_info Extension
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new TLS extension, renegotiation_info, with extension type 0xff01, which carries a cryptographic binding to the enclosing TLS connection, if any, for which the renegotiation is being performed. The extension data field contains a RenegotiationInfo structure, which holds a single opaque field renegotiated_connection of up to 255 bytes.

The contents are as follows. If this is the initial handshake for a connection, the renegotiated_connection field is of zero length in both the ClientHello and the ServerHello, so the entire encoding of the extension is ff 01 00 01 00: the first two octets are the extension type, the third and fourth the length of the extension itself, and the final octet the zero-length byte for the field. For a ClientHello that is renegotiating, the field contains the client_verify_data. For a ServerHello that is renegotiating, it contains the concatenation of client_verify_data and server_verify_data, which for current versions of TLS is a 24-byte value, or 72 bytes for SSLv3.

The extension can also be used with Datagram TLS. For editorial simplicity the document refers to TLS, but all of its requirements apply equally to DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is a short block of bytes added to the handshake. In the first handshake it is empty, which simply says that both ends support the safe form; in a later handshake it carries the values that ended the previous handshake, so a mismatch gives the attack away.

sections.title: A Second Way to Signal Support
sections.content:
Both the SSLv3 and the TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 specifications require implementations to ignore data following the ClientHello if they do not understand it, but some SSLv3 and TLS 1.0 implementations incorrectly fail the handshake in such a case. A client that offers the renegotiation_info extension may therefore encounter handshake failures.

To improve compatibility with such servers, the RFC defines a second signalling mechanism: the special signalling cipher suite value TLS_EMPTY_RENEGOTIATION_INFO_SCSV, with code point {0x00, 0xFF}. It is not a true cipher suite, it does not correspond to any valid set of algorithms and cannot be negotiated. Instead it has the same semantics as an empty renegotiation_info extension. Because SSLv3 and TLS implementations reliably ignore unknown cipher suites, the SCSV may safely be sent to any server, and it can also be included in the SSLv2 backward compatible CLIENT-HELLO.

A minimal client that does not support renegotiation at all can simply use the SCSV in all initial handshakes, and the rules that follow will cause any compliant server to abort the handshake when it sees an apparent attempt at renegotiation by such a client.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older servers break when they see an extension they do not know. To avoid that, a second signal is provided: a reserved cipher suite value that every server safely ignores but that still tells a modern server that the client supports the safe form.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
For an initial handshake, which includes session resumption, the client must include either an empty renegotiation_info extension or the TLS_EMPTY_RENEGOTIATION_INFO_SCSV signalling cipher suite value in the ClientHello; including both is not recommended. When the ServerHello arrives, the client must check whether it includes the extension. If it does not, the server does not support secure renegotiation, and the client sets the secure_renegotiation flag to FALSE; some clients may prefer to terminate the handshake instead. If the extension is present, the client sets the flag to TRUE and must verify that the length of the renegotiated_connection field is zero, aborting the handshake with a fatal handshake_failure alert if it is not. Once the handshake completes, the client saves the client_verify_data and server_verify_data values for future use.

For a secure renegotiation, the client must include the renegotiation_info extension in the ClientHello, containing the saved client_verify_data, and must not include the SCSV. When the ServerHello arrives, the client must verify that the extension is present and abort the handshake if it is not. It must then verify that the first half of the renegotiated_connection field equals the saved client_verify_data and that the second half equals the saved server_verify_data, aborting if they are not. After the handshake completes, the client saves the new values.
sections.plainLanguage: On the first handshake the client offers the extension and checks that the server echoes it back empty. On a later handshake the client quotes the values from the previous handshake and checks that the server quotes exactly the same ones.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
For an initial handshake, the server must check whether the ClientHello includes the TLS_EMPTY_RENEGOTIATION_INFO_SCSV, and set the secure_renegotiation flag to TRUE if it does. It must also check whether the renegotiation_info extension is included; if it is, the server sets the flag to TRUE and must verify that the length of the renegotiated_connection field is zero, aborting the handshake if it is not. If neither the SCSV nor the extension was included, the server sets the flag to FALSE, and some servers may prefer to terminate the handshake instead. If the flag is TRUE, the server must include an empty renegotiation_info extension in the ServerHello. Once the handshake completes, the server saves the two verify data values.

The RFC restates two requirements from RFC 5246 in the interest of forward compatibility: TLS servers implementing this specification must ignore any unknown extensions offered by the client, and they must accept version numbers higher than their own and negotiate the highest common version. Sending a renegotiation_info extension in response to a ClientHello that contained only the SCSV is an explicit exception to the rule in RFC 5246 that a server must not send unsolicited extensions, and it is allowed only because the client signalled its willingness with the SCSV.

For a secure renegotiation, the server must verify that the ClientHello does not contain the SCSV, and abort the handshake if it does. It must verify that the renegotiation_info extension is present and abort if it is not. It must verify that the value of the renegotiated_connection field equals the saved client_verify_data, and abort if it does not. It must then include a renegotiation_info extension containing the saved client_verify_data and server_verify_data in the ServerHello, and save the new values when the handshake completes.
sections.plainLanguage: The server does the same checks in the other direction. The important one is on a renegotiation: the value the client quotes must match the value the server remembers, and if it does not, the server ends the connection.

sections.title: Talking to Older Servers
sections.content:
Existing implementations that do not support the extension are widely deployed and must interoperate with newer ones, so the RFC sets out how each side should behave.

On the client side, if the client offers the extension or the SCSV and the server does not reply with the extension in the ServerHello, the server does not support secure renegotiation. Because some attacks look like a single handshake to the client, the client cannot tell whether the connection is under attack. Not receiving the extension does not mean the server is vulnerable; it may simply reject all renegotiations without signalling that. If clients wish to make such attacks impossible, they need to terminate the connection immediately upon failing to receive the extension, sending a fatal handshake_failure alert first, but many TLS servers that do not support renegotiation will not support the extension either, so such clients will meet interoperability problems. There is no client behaviour that guarantees both security and maximum interoperability during the transition, and clients must choose one or the other.

If the flag is FALSE, it is possible that an un-upgraded server will ask the client to renegotiate, and it is recommended that clients refuse, answering with a no_renegotiation alert at the warning level. The apparently un-upgraded server may in fact be an attacker allowing the client to renegotiate with a different, legitimate, upgraded server. If clients do choose to renegotiate, they must provide either the SCSV or the extension in the ClientHello; a legitimate un-upgraded server should ignore both, but if it fails to ignore extensions, sending the extension may cause a handshake failure, so it is permitted though not recommended for the client simply to send the SCSV. That is the only situation in which a client may omit the extension in a renegotiating ClientHello. The client must then verify that the ServerHello does not contain the extension, and abort if it does, since the server has already said it does not support secure renegotiation and the only other explanation is a broken server or an attack.

On the server side, a client that offers neither the extension nor the SCSV does not support secure renegotiation. Although the attack looks like two handshakes to the server, other attacks may exist in which only the client sees a renegotiation. A server that wants to make such attacks impossible must terminate the connection when secure renegotiation is not negotiated, and a server that does allow unpatched clients can still prevent the attack by refusing to renegotiate over those connections. So that clients can probe, even servers that do not support renegotiation must implement the minimal version of the extension for initial handshakes, signalling that they have been upgraded.

SSLv3 is not a protocol under IETF change control, but it was the original basis for TLS and most implementations also support it. The IETF encourages SSLv3 implementations to adopt the extension and the SCSV, with the same semantics except that the verify data values are 36 bytes each. SSLv3 does not define the no_renegotiation alert, so SSLv3 clients that refuse renegotiation should use a fatal handshake_failure alert.
sections.plainLanguage: Older servers are everywhere, so the RFC says what to do when the other end does not answer with the extension: either keep going and accept the risk, or refuse the connection. It also says a server should refuse to renegotiate on a connection where the client did not offer the extension at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension prevents an attack on TLS. Without it, renegotiation is subject to an attack in which the attacker injects their own conversation with the server as a prefix to the client's conversation. That attack is invisible to the client and looks like an ordinary renegotiation to the server. Servers should not allow clients to renegotiate without using the extension, and many servers can mitigate the attack simply by refusing to renegotiate at all.

The extension does not resolve every problem an application may face if it is unaware of renegotiation. During a renegotiation either the client or the server can present a different certificate from the one used earlier, which may surprise application developers who might have expected a call such as getPeerCertificates to return the same value when called twice, and may be handled in an insecure way. TLS implementations should provide a mechanism to disable and to enable renegotiation, and implementers are encouraged to document clearly how renegotiation interacts with the interfaces offered to applications, for example which calls might return different values on different calls or which callbacks might be invoked more than once.

To make life simpler for applications that use renegotiation but do not expect the certificate to change once it has been authenticated, implementations may offer the option to abort the renegotiation if the peer tries to authenticate with a different certificate or a different server name in the server_name extension than was used earlier, or the option to disable renegotiation once the client certificate has been authenticated. Enabling those options by default could break existing applications that depend on renegotiation to change from one certificate to another, for example a long-lived connection that moves to a renewed certificate, or a renegotiation that selects a different cipher suite needing a different certificate.

Finally, designers of applications that depend on renegotiation are reminded that many TLS interfaces present application data as a simple octet stream, so an application may not be able to determine exactly which data octets arrived before, during or after a renegotiation. Care is needed in specifying how the application should handle the data, especially if the peer presents a different certificate during the renegotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix stops the splicing attack, but it does not stop an application from being surprised when a renegotiation brings a different certificate. The RFC asks implementations to say plainly how renegotiation shows up in their interfaces, and to give applications the choice of refusing a certificate change.
